extracted.intended_audience: poets, critics, and literary students (young authors and readers interested in poetic theory)
extracted.subtask_description: Critical criteria and practical guidance for composing and evaluating poetry, especially poetic diction, style, and the relationship of thought and language as articulated by Samuel Taylor Coleridge in Biographia Literaria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Returnability as essential poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: “Not the poem which we have read, but that to which we return, with the greatest pleasure, possesses the genuine power, and claims the name of essential poetry.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A poem's lasting power is measured by the pleasure it yields on repeated readings; the true test of a poem's merit is whether readers return to it, not merely initial impressiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unparaphrasability / indivisibility of poetic diction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Whatever lines can be translated into other words of the same language, without diminution of their significance, either in sense or association, or in any worthy feeling, are so far vicious in their diction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetic lines should resist simple paraphrase; if meaning, associations, or feeling survive unchanged when reworded, the diction is defective. This is a test of precision and the inseparability of form and sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturalness and austerity of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for an “austerer and more natural style” and praise of those who “combined natural thoughts with natural diction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor plain, natural language over ornate, artificial ornamentation. Natural diction reconciles feeling and thought and is preferable to florid or excessively affected expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: Obscurity was a frequent criticism of youthful poems and is described as a fault a writer often cannot detect in his own compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should be wary of obscurity in thought or expression; clarity suited to the nature and objects of poetry is valued over unintelligible complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy: reason for every word and position
rubrics_metrics.description: “In the truly great poets... there is a reason assignable, not only for every word, but for the position of every word.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose each word deliberately; the placement and choice of words should be justified by sense, tone, and effect—altering a word or its position often changes the poet's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unsupported phrase, metaphor, or image
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases, metaphors, or images unsupported by a sound sense, or where the same sense might have been conveyed in plainer words, were subject to severe censure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor and image must be grounded in sense and necessity; ornamental images without supporting meaning should be eliminated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject hackneyed stock-phrases and similes
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge recounts an index of interdicted introductions, similes, and familiar phrases (e.g., harp, lyre, Muse, Pegasus, Alexander and Clytus) as an abomination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid clichéd or overused classical/stock tropes and similes; such phrases often dilute originality and literary force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of passion and intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between older poets (sacrificing passion to wit) and moderns (sacrificing heart and head to point and drapery); poetry should reconcile heart with head.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a balance where feeling and intellect cohere—neither pure intellectual wit at the expense of emotion nor mere ornamented cleverness without depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against translating prose thoughts into verse
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of poetry that is merely 'translations of prose thoughts into poetic language'; such poetry lacks genuine poetic thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poems should originate in genuinely poetic thought, not be prose ideas dressed in verse; the matter must be poetic in kind, not only in presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject novelty for novelty's sake
rubrics_metrics.description: Coleridge excludes from worthy feelings 'the pleasure derived from mere novelty in the reader, and the desire of exciting wonderment at his powers in the author.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovation should not be pursued as an end to thrill the reader; novelty that substitutes for genuine feeling or thought is a defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meter imposes dictional constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: “Language of metrical composition, why and wherein essentially different from that of prose—Origin and elements of metre—Its necessary consequences, and the conditions thereby imposed on the metrical writer in the choice of his diction.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing verse, choose diction that fits metrical requirements; metre constrains word choice and syntax, and the poet must select language suited to metrical form while preserving sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected or false simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of 'low creeping language and thoughts, under the pretence of simplicity' and of 'affected simplicity' as one of the sins of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity must be genuine—simple language that conceals poverty of thought or is a pose is to be shunned; simplicity should arise from truth of feeling and thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prune excessive ornament and swollen diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Author admits pruning 'double epithets' and taming 'the swell and glitter both of thought and diction'; excess of ornament was a youthful fault.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revise to remove excessive epithets, glittering ornament, and inflated diction; trimming embellishment often improves clarity and force.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical pedagogy: eliminate repeated faults
rubrics_metrics.description: Anecdote of a teacher who would tear up an exercise if two faults of the same kind occurred and require a new exercise instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use strict revision discipline: repeated identical faults indicate insufficient correction—address and eliminate recurring weaknesses rather than ignore them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry has its own rigorous internal logic
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry... had a logic of its own, as severe as that of science; and more difficult, because more subtle, more complex, and dependent on more, and more fugitive causes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure internal consistency, coherence, and logical order in poetic structure and argument; poetic logic governs appropriateness of diction, imagery, and progression of thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid egotism, repetitious favourite phrases, and self-indulgence
rubrics_metrics.description: Denunciation of 'doleful egotism' and recurrence of favourite phrases that are at once trite and licentious; these are among the sins of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of self-indulgent recurring phrases and egotistic turns that appeal only to the author's vanity; variety and self-awareness are necessary.
